rationale:
Seed for collaborators: the round-2 champion of the squidpy experiment (r2-v4, sha256:d2dd6655d1476cc61ecbdf60872d27022158b050eef2ed4408ed861bc7c33c0d), lockbox mean 27/36 over 2 clean drafts vs a 22/36 no-skill floor. Chain r1-v1 -> r1-v2 (round 1 pick) -> r2-v1 (re-seed) -> r2-v4 (round 2 pick). Its own rationale, verbatim:

## What changed

Added a new bullet, "Don't transplant the tutorial's incidental setup onto every task," and
added a clarifying clause to the existing "rank X" bullet that points back to it. Also added
one clause to "Test sensitivity, not just existence" calling out chunked/tiled image-processing
parameters as another axis worth testing.

## Why (train evidence)

The single largest failure cluster on train (8 of 18 failing runs, all "which gene has the
strongest spatial autocorrelation" style tasks) had a consistent, checkable cause: the drafted
skill's body, following the existing "Don't trust a precomputed column" and "pin down the exact
recipe / reproduce the package's worked example exactly" bullets, led agents to recompute and
restrict to a highly-variable-gene subset before ranking genes by Moran's I — even on tasks
whose wording never asked for any gene restriction. Two of the passing runs for the *same*
dataset and computation used the full gene set exactly as shipped and got the ground-truth gene;
every failing run that added an unrequested HVG recompute/restriction got a different (wrong)
top gene. The same shape of mistake showed up in a segmentation-count task: the task never
mentioned cropping the image, but the agent cropped it anyway to the specific region used by an
unrelated tutorial notebook, producing a count nowhere near the true one (expected count matched
running on the full, uncropped image). In both cases the existing "reproduce the exact recipe"
instruction was being over-applied: it correctly says to copy the package's function sequence and
parameter conventions, but the drafted skills were also copying that example's incidental,
example-only choices (which gene-count cutoff, which crop region) and treating them as a general
default to apply on every task, even ones that never asked for that step at all. The new bullet
names this failure mode directly and tells the drafter to separate "the recipe" from "the
example's own incidental setup," and to only add a restriction/crop/extra-preprocessing step when
the task's own wording calls for it. The chunked-processing note comes from a paired failure
(same image, same segmentation call, only a tile-size parameter differed) that produced two
different object counts — a second, narrower instance of the same "invisible parameter changes
the answer" family already covered by "Test sensitivity," so it was added as one more example
there rather than a new bullet.

I did not touch the pair-ordering bullet despite four related failures: two pairs of train tasks
expected opposite name orders for what looks like the identical underlying computation on the
identical bundled dataset, which suggests that ambiguity is noise in how each task's ground truth
was generated rather than something a rulebook instruction can resolve — sharpening that bullet
further risks tuning to one task's arbitrary order at the expense of another's opposite one.
